Shoot before you buy. This is really the best advice that can be offered. You will not have any idea how much you will like or dislike a particular firearm until you have held and fired it. There are some I thought I would love and just can't stand. I thought the Chippa Rhino was going to be awesome, until I shot it. I hate just about everything about that gun. I also just cant get used to the Glock trigger, but some people like my sister have no problem with it. Be prepared to spend some money test driving. Ranges will differ on how the rentals are done, you will just need to ask around in your area. For example, the range closest to me has 2 tiers of rentals. $25 for the first tier, can shoot any gun in that tier and swap as much as you want, but you have to use their ammo. $35 for both first and second tier. Another range is $5 per gun, but again you have to use their ammo. Range ammo will typically be a little more expensive by a few dollars a box than what you can pick up on your own. I would not advise that you go any smaller than .380 or .38 special for a carry gun. 9mm is a good balance, but if you go bigger to .40 or .45 you get heavier and start to lose round capacity. Also keep in mind that a lighter gun will be harder to control. The weight helps to tame recoil and keep you closer to on target, where a small gun can be jumpy even in the lighter calibers. If a malfunction occurs on a semi-auto, you have a bit of a process to go through to get the gun back into action. Sometimes needing as much as to drop the mag, rack the slide, reinsert the mag and then rack again to chamber a round. But you have ease of reloading if everything goes smoothly and higher capacities. If a malfunction occurs on a revolver, you just pull the trigger again. Also, most chamberings will allow multiple cartridges. For example, a .357 will also chamber .38 special. The downside is that capacity will be less (6-8 rounds) and reloading can take longer even with a speed loader. If you want to do some research, I would advise you watch Hickok45 on youtube. He has reviews for so many guns and goes into detail about the pros and cons of each. He used to be a school teacher and it shows in how his videos are presented. Good affordable makes are CZ, S&W, Ruger, Sig, and Glock. The model will depend on what you are able to handle and shoot competently. If you find one you like and shoot well, before you buy, research that particular model. Even reputable manufactures put out some lemons from time to time, but in general something from the brands above will most likely be good to go.

First off, all of the smaller lighter firearms are typically going to have more recoil. Go to a store, hold a few that are suggested in the comments and take note, then go to a range and rent the ones that felt the best in your hands. Put the target no more than 2m/12 feet than you and systematically test the firearms you chose. This shouldn't be a quick process, take the time you have with what you rented to get a feel for them. If you're not used to them indoor ranges can be nerve racking, so if you feel overwhelmed finish up and do it again. Also, don't worry too much about "powerful", the majority of firearms will take someone down if placed in center mass unless they're on PCP. I might get some flack for this but IMO a .22 that you can operate is more useful to you than a .50 that you can't. In the end you'll probably settle on a 32 acp, 380, or a 9 mm if you decide on a semi auto.

Revolver: If you're inexperienced and want to just pull the trigger in a panic get a double action only revolver without a safety such as the Smith and Wesson M&P bodyguard. If you're in a situation and haven't trained all you have to do is point and pull the trigger, and if you get a dud you can just keep pulling the trigger without having to "rack tap bang". The downsides to a firearm like this is limited ammo capacity, the one mentioned above only has 5 rounds, recoil, the trigger pull weight is much higher (it's harder to pull the trigger), and they're a bit fatter than semi autos. If you need to reload it, it's going to take a while unless you carry a speed loader with you.

Semi auto: These will give you more rounds, and the ability to reload much faster assuming you carry spare magazines with you. The Ruger LC9s is great and I've heard great things about the Glock 43. These will be a bit slimmer than the revolvers and probably be a bit easier to shoot since the trigger pull weight is much lighter, and it also depends on then firearm and if you carry it with one in the chamber. For example, if you carried the Glock 43 with a round in the chamber it's going to be ready to go since it has no physical safety switch unless you experience a misfire/jam in which case you're going to need to "rack tap bang". If you carried without one in the chamber you're going to need to rack it and possibly disengage the safety if you carry with it engaged.

Side note on the revolver vs semi autos: If you get a CCW and a CCW purse, a double action only revolver will not get jammed if you feel the need to fire it from inside your purse while there is a high probability that a semi auto will jam depending on the construction of the CCW pocket in the purse.
